About

Who we are.

A small Episcopal parish on the coast of Maine, gathered for worship since 1849 — and still trying to figure out what that means.

A welcome from the Rector

“Stay for coffee.”

When you walk in for the first time, I will probably be at the door. I'll say good morning and hand you a bulletin. I will not ask you about your beliefs or your bank account or whether you've been baptized. I will ask if I can save you a seat, or if you'd like to sit alone for a while, which is also a perfectly fine reason to come to church.

St. Brendan's is small and old and a little drafty. We are not slick. We sing some of the hymns very well, and we miss notes on others. The sermon does not always land. The coffee in the parish hall is usually pretty good, though, and the people are kind, and the cove out the window is one of the most beautiful things in the state of Maine.

What we are trying to do here, week after week, is pray honestly — about the world, about our own lives, about people we love and people we have failed to love. We are trying to read the gospels carefully and listen to what they have to say, even when what they have to say is uncomfortable. We are trying to take care of one another and of our small piece of the coast.

You do not need to believe anything in particular to come and try this with us. You don't need to be Episcopalian, or any kind of Christian, or sure of anything at all. You need to be willing to sit down with people who are trying. That's the whole prerequisite. Come and see, as Philip said to Nathanael. And then stay for coffee.

— The Rev. Hannah Wycliffe, Rector

To gather as a community of prayer on this harbor,
to share the bread and cup of Christ,
and to be useful to our neighbors —
as long as we have breath.
Our mission, adopted 2014
Our history

Founded in 1849.

St. Brendan's was founded in October of 1849 by a group of fifteen families in what was then the village of Kettle Cove, a working harbor for the coastal schooners that ran timber and salt cod up and down the coast. The first services were held in the parlor of Captain Ezekiel Tasker's house on School Street, with a circuit-riding priest from the parish in Portland coming up once a month to celebrate the Eucharist. The rest of the Sundays were Morning Prayer, led by Tasker or one of the other lay readers.

The current building was consecrated on Easter Day, 1872, by the Right Reverend Henry A. Neely, the second Bishop of Maine. It is a Carpenter Gothic frame church — white clapboard, steep slate roof, a single steeple with a small bell — built by local shipwrights on a piece of granite ledge that gives the nave its slight pitch toward the altar. The pews are the original chestnut, scarred and oiled by a century and a half of use. The harbor window above the altar, depicting the boat in the storm on the Sea of Galilee, was added in 1894 in memory of three local fishermen lost off the Brendan Ledges, the rocks from which the parish takes its name.

The twentieth century was, by turns, generous and hard. The parish was strong through the 1950s, with three Sunday services and a full Sunday School. The 1970s and 80s brought the slow erosion that small coastal parishes know — younger people moving inland for work, the summer-only houses growing in number. The roof leaked badly through most of the 1990s. In 1998, after a capital campaign that nearly doubled the giving of the parish, the slate roof was rebuilt by a small crew of slaters out of New Brunswick, the harbor window restored, and the foundation re-pointed.

The twenty-first century has been a steadier story. We are about the size we were in 1925 — one hundred and forty active members, somewhat older on average than we would like, but with new families finding us each year. We received our first openly gay member in 2003 and have not been the same parish since, in the best ways. The Rev. Hannah Wycliffe arrived as Rector in 2019, becoming the first woman to hold the position. We weathered the pandemic with online Morning Prayer and a great many phone calls; we lost a few beloved members and gained a surprising number of new ones who'd been worshiping with us on screens from elsewhere on the coast.

The parish hall, behind the church, was added in 1961 and houses our kitchen, a meeting room, the church office, and the staffed nursery. The columbarium garden was added in 2009 and is now home to a small grove of memorial yews. The building is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Clergy

The Rev. Hannah Wycliffe & the Rev. Marcus Adlersson.

The Rev. Hannah Wycliffe

Rector · since 2019

Hannah grew up in Hartford, Connecticut, the third of four children of a high-school music teacher and a public defender. She came to the Episcopal Church in her early twenties by way of an Easter Vigil at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York, and never quite recovered. She holds a B.A. from Wesleyan University in religion and music, and an M.Div. from Berkeley Divinity School at Yale.

She was ordained a deacon in the Diocese of Connecticut in 2002 and a priest in 2003, and served for the next sixteen years in two parishes: as Curate at Christ Church, New Haven, and then as Rector of the Church of the Resurrection in a small mill town in northern Massachusetts, where she led the parish through a difficult building project and learned most of what she knows about pastoral ministry.

She came to St. Brendan's in the fall of 2019, called by the search committee partly for her experience with small parishes and partly because she was the only candidate who knew, on sight, that the bird on the church lawn was a yellow-rumped warbler. She lives in the rectory next door with her wife, Mira, a marine biologist who works for the Gulf of Maine Research Institute, and their elderly black lab, Augustine.

Hannah's theological convictions are broad-church Anglican: deeply sacramental, generously orthodox, persuaded that the gospel is good news and not finally about scorekeeping. She is a long-time reader of Rowan Williams, Sara Miles, and Marilynne Robinson, and is increasingly persuaded by the writings of the late Sam Wells on what he calls “being with” as the heart of Christian ministry. She preaches without notes on most Sundays and writes a brief weekly note to the parish on Friday afternoons.

You can reach her at rector@stbrendanskettlecove.org, or by calling the parish office. Her sabbath day is Friday and she does her best to take it.

The Rev. Marcus Adlersson

Curate · part-time

Marcus came to St. Brendan's in 2024 as our first curate in nearly two decades, following his ordination to the diaconate and priesthood at the cathedral in Portland. He grew up in Bar Harbor, the son of a Swedish-born boat carpenter and a Penobscot-side ceramicist, and is one of the few clergy in the diocese who can identify a Friendship sloop at a hundred yards.

Before seminary at Virginia Theological Seminary, Marcus worked as a wilderness therapy guide in Maine and Wyoming and as a part-time youth minister at the parish of his childhood. His doctoral work focused on what he calls “coastal ecclesiology” — the ways small harbor churches have shaped, and been shaped by, the ecological and economic lives of the communities around them.

He serves the parish on Sundays, midweek, and one day during the week, while also working part-time as a chaplain at the Kettle Cove regional hospital. He preaches monthly, leads our adult formation program, and has been the driving force behind the summer evensong series at the town landing.

Lay staff

The people who keep the building open.

Phoebe Larkins

Music Director & Organist

Phoebe has led the music ministry since 2011. A graduate of Eastman, she directs the choir, plays the 1968 Casavant organ, and accompanies the children's Sunday morning singing with what she calls “more patience than skill” (we disagree).

Theodore O'Connell

Parish Administrator

Ted runs the church office, the bulletin, the building schedule, and most other things you might think the clergy run. He is here Tuesday through Friday, 9 AM to 1 PM. If you need a key, a calendar slot, or a printer that works, Ted is who you want.

Bill Brewster

Sexton

Bill has cared for the building and grounds since 2003. He opens the church before dawn most mornings, plows the lot in winter, and rings the bell at the start of the principal service most Sundays. He knows every leak the church has ever had.

Vestry

Lay leadership of the parish.

The wider church

The Diocese of Maine.

St. Brendan's is one of about sixty congregations in the Episcopal Diocese of Maine, a member diocese of The Episcopal Church — itself a province of the worldwide Anglican Communion. Our bishop is the Right Reverend Sarah Whitcombe-Vance, the eleventh Bishop of Maine. The diocesan office and cathedral (the Cathedral Church of St. Luke) are in Portland.

We send delegates to the annual Diocesan Convention, contribute a fair-share assessment to the work of the diocese (campus ministries, retreat centers, support for smaller parishes), and welcome our bishop for a visitation roughly every eighteen months — her visits typically include confirmations, baptisms, and the reception of any new members coming to us from other traditions.

Learn more about the diocese at episcopalmaine.org, and about the Episcopal Church at episcopalchurch.org.

Our welcome

You are welcome here.

St. Brendan's is an affirming congregation. We welcome to full participation in the life and leadership of this parish all people, without regard to race, color, ethnic origin, national origin, citizenship, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital or family status, age, disability, socioeconomic status, or theological background.

That means: same-sex couples are married here. Transgender and non-binary members serve on the vestry, lead worship, and read scripture. Children are not asked to be quiet; they are asked to be themselves. Newcomers are welcomed by name. People who have been hurt by the church before are believed when they tell us so, and we will work to do better.

Our building is accessible. The nave has step-free entry from the parking lot; the side aisle accommodates a wheelchair through the entire service, including communion at the altar rail. The hearing loop covers most of the seating; switch your hearing aid to T-coil. Large-print bulletins and Hymnals are available from the ushers. Both restrooms are gender-neutral; one is fully accessible. A quiet room with a closed-circuit audio feed is available at the back of the parish hall.

If there is something we have missed — some way we could welcome you that we have not yet thought of — please tell us. We will listen.
